opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Today, most of the critical feedback a project gets arrives very late. You spend months, sometimes a year or more, developing an idea, running experiments, writing the paper, and only then does it go out to reviewers. By that point a lot of the key decisions are baked in: the experimental design, the controls you chose, the datasets you used. If a reviewer points out a fundamental flaw, it's very expensive to go back and fix it.

Lab meetings are where those early decisions actually get made, when a student presents a half-formed idea or a first set of results. The quality of the critique at that stage depends heavily on who happens to be in the room. If nobody has the right expertise, or people are too polite, or everyone is busy with their own projects, important weaknesses slip through.

That's part of why we've been interested in AI agents as critics, including in the Virtual Lab work, where we had a dedicated critic agent whose whole role was to poke holes in the plans the other agents proposed. What we found is that having that critical voice built into the process, rather than bolted on at the end, makes the overall output more rigorous. The critic catches things like missing baselines, overclaimed conclusions, or alternative explanations nobody considered.

Moving that into real human lab meetings, you could imagine an AI that reads the slides or draft beforehand and raises the questions a tough reviewer would ask, but at a point where you can still change course cheaply. It also democratizes things a bit. A student at a small lab without a big group of senior colleagues can get the kind of tough, constructive pushback that's usually only available in large, well-resourced groups.

To be clear, the goal isn't to replace human judgment or discourage people from exploring bold ideas. It's to shift the feedback loop earlier, so we spend less time going down paths that a careful critic could have flagged on day one.

r001.rationale: The response says people in lab meetings may be “too polite,” allowing weaknesses to slip through, which suggests they may leave criticisms unspoken.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way most labs work right now is that critique comes in pretty late. You do the project, you write it up, you submit it, and then the reviewers tell you what's wrong with it. And by that point you've already sunk months into the thing, so you're mostly in a defensive mode. You're trying to patch it up rather than really rethink it.

And what we've been experimenting with, partly with AI agents and partly just as a cultural thing in the lab, is to pull that critical voice forward. So when someone is presenting an early idea in lab meeting, maybe they've only been on it for a week or two, we already ask: what's the strongest objection to this? What would a skeptical reviewer say? Is there an existing baseline that already does this? Is the evaluation actually measuring what you claim it's measuring?

There are a couple of reasons I think this is valuable. One is just efficiency. It's much cheaper to kill or redirect a project at week two than at month six. A lot of the critiques that reviewers eventually raise are actually pretty predictable, and if you surface them early you either fix the design or you realize the idea isn't as strong as you thought.

The second reason is more subtle. When you get critique early, before you're emotionally invested, it's much easier to take it seriously. People are more open-minded about an idea they've had for a week than one they've spent half a year on. So the same comment lands very differently depending on when it's delivered.

And the third thing, which I find really interesting, is that it changes what students learn. If critique only shows up at the end, students mostly learn how to defend work. If it shows up at the beginning, they learn how to anticipate it, and eventually they internalize that voice themselves. That's really what you want. You want researchers who are their own harshest reviewer at the design stage, not people who find out what's wrong from a rejection letter.

The one caveat is you have to be careful about tone, because early-stage ideas are fragile. The goal isn't to shoot everything down, it's to stress test. So we try to frame it as, here are the things this project needs to survive, rather than, here's why it won't work. But done right, I think it's one of the highest leverage changes you can make to how a lab operates.

r001.rationale: The response advocates surfacing criticism earlier and mentions being careful with tone, but it does not say that lab meeting participants may keep privately held criticisms unspoken.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s valuable because early in a project, you still have a lot of flexibility to change direction. If somebody raises a concern about an assumption, or points out that an experiment wouldn’t actually support the claim you want to make, you can address that before you’ve invested months of work.

And ideally, that becomes part of the culture of the lab meeting. You’re not just presenting results and hoping everybody likes them. You’re asking, “What are we missing? What would convince us that our interpretation is wrong?” That makes criticism a contribution to the project, and it gives you a chance to make the science stronger while it’s still taking shape.

r001.rationale: The response encourages participants to raise concerns and ask critical questions, but it does not say that they may privately hold criticisms and leave them unspoken.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s valuable because early in a project, you still have a lot of flexibility to change direction. If critical feedback only comes when you submit the paper, you might have spent a year building around an assumption that somebody could have challenged at the beginning.

So in a lab meeting, we can ask: What’s the strongest argument against this idea? Are we actually testing the claim we want to make? What result would convince us that we’re wrong? That can help us design better experiments and identify limitations earlier. And if that’s a regular part of the conversation, it becomes easier to treat criticism as a way to improve the work rather than as a judgment of the person doing it.

r001.rationale: The response advocates inviting criticism earlier, but does not say that lab meeting participants may keep criticisms they privately hold unspoken.
